body:
The per-(user, book) annotation backup is the safety net that the recoverability
argument for every destructive annotation path leans on. Two properties limit
what it can actually recover, and they compound.

1. RETENTION IS COUNT-BASED, AND A LOSS EVENT SPENDS ITS OWN SLOTS
`RETENTION_COUNT = 3` (cps/services/annotation_backup.py:57). `_apply_retention`
(:331) keeps the newest three by `created_at DESC` and UNLINKS the file for each
older one. Backups are content-hash deduped (:222), so only content-CHANGING
events consume a slot — but a destructive push is exactly such an event. Three
content-changing writes after a loss and the last snapshot that still held the
lost annotation is deleted from disk permanently. The window is three events,
not three days, and the event that caused the loss is the first to spend one.

2. THERE IS NO RESTORE PATH
The schema-version comment at :51 says a restore endpoint is a "(future PR)".
Grepping the tree confirms none exists: `restore_annotation_device`
(cps/annotations.py:181) restores DEVICE ASSIGNMENT ROUTING, not annotation
content, and the admin restore at cps/admin.py:3568 is the Calibre-database last
resort that explicitly ERASES all per-book data. So today the gzip snapshots are
written, retained and evicted, and cannot be loaded back through any application
path.

WHAT IS AND IS NOT AFFECTED
- Soft-deleted rows are still IN the backup: `_run_one` selects all rows for the
  pair with no `hidden` filter (:204), so a `hidden=True` row keeps its content.
  Those rows are also still in the live DB, so the backup is not the only copy.
- A HARD delete is the real exposure. F-a7b6b2 (duplicate-book merge) removes the
  row from the DB entirely, so a pre-merge snapshot is the ONLY copy — and it is
  subject to both limits above.

SEVERITY FRAMING (stated honestly)
The missing restore endpoint is deferred deliberately, not an accident, so this
is not filed as a defect in itself. What is actionable NOW, independent of that
endpoint, is limit 1: eviction is blind to what a snapshot contains. A snapshot
holding annotations that no longer exist in the live DB is precisely the one
worth keeping, and it is currently the first to be unlinked.

SUGGESTED DIRECTION (not a spec)
Make retention content-aware rather than purely count-based — e.g. never evict
the most recent snapshot whose annotation set is not a subset of the live set,
so the last pre-loss state survives until a restore path exists to use it.
title: Annotation backup retention is count-based and evicts the pre-loss snapshot, and no restore path exists to use one
